title: Qixian, Shanxi: A Buyer’s Guide to China’s Hand-Blown Glassware Capital
excerpt: Qixian County in Shanxi produces over 60% of China’s hand-blown glassware and exports more than 70% of it to 80+ countries. Here is what that means for importers.
body:
**Short answer:** Qixian County (祁县) in Jinzhong, Shanxi Province, is China’s core production area for hand-blown glassware. It accounts for more than 60% of national hand-blown output, and over 70% of its products are exported to more than 80 countries and regions, according to a February 2026 Xinhua report.

## Key facts about the Qixian glassware cluster

| Fact | Figure | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Share of China’s hand-blown glassware output | over 60% | Xinhua, Feb 2026 |
| Share of output exported | over 70% | Xinhua, Feb 2026 |
| Export destinations | 80+ countries and regions | Xinhua, Feb 2026 |
| Glassware manufacturers | 62, plus 230+ upstream/downstream firms | Xinhua, Feb 2026 |
| Local workers in glass-blowing | about 30,000 | Xinhua, Feb 2026 |
| Quality infrastructure | national-level glassware quality inspection center | Xinhua, Feb 2026 |

## How the industry started
Local historians trace the craft to Shanxi merchants who traded along the Ming–Qing "tea road" across Eurasia and brought glass-blowing techniques back home. More than a century later the county has a full supply chain: raw materials, molds, furnaces, decoration, packaging and export logistics.

## What Qixian is good at
- **Hand-blown stemware and decanters**: thin rims, pulled stems and complex shapes that machines cannot make economically
- **Colored and decorative glass**: ombre, overlay, patterned stems, gold decoration, styles popular in Europe and the Middle East
- **Small-batch flexibility**: hand production allows lower MOQs and faster design changes than fully automated plants
- **Borosilicate**: newer automated lines now produce heat-resistant glassware at scale

## What to check before you order
1. **Process match**: hand-blown, mold-blown or machine-pressed? Each factory specializes.
2. **Glass type**: soda-lime, lead-free crystal or borosilicate, which affects clarity, weight and price.
3. **Tolerance**: hand-made items vary slightly; agree on acceptable ranges for height, weight and capacity.
4. **Packaging**: glass needs drop-tested export cartons; confirm this in the quotation.
5. **Inspection**: insist on pre-shipment QC with photos.

## Why work with a local sourcing partner
With dozens of factories each focusing on different processes, the fastest route is a local team that already knows which workshop makes which product well. We visit the factories, compare quotations, follow production and inspect goods before they leave Shanxi.

*Source: Xinhua, "Glass-blowing craft thrives in China's ancient county", 21 Feb 2026.*

title: Hand-Blown vs Machine-Made Glassware: Which Is Right for Your Market?
excerpt: Choose hand-blown glass for premium, thin-rim or small-batch designs; choose machine-made for high volume, consistent sizes and lower unit cost.
body:
**Short answer:** Hand-blown glassware suits premium positioning, thin rims, unusual shapes and small batches. Machine-made glassware suits high volumes, tight size consistency and the lowest unit cost.

## Side-by-side comparison

| Factor | Hand-blown | Machine-made |
|---|---|---|
| Typical MOQ | 300–1,000 pcs | 3,000–10,000+ pcs |
| Unit cost | Higher | Lower |
| Rim | Can be very thin (≈1 mm), cut and polished | Usually thicker, rolled or fire-polished |
| Size consistency | Small variations | Very consistent |
| Design flexibility | High, quick changes | Needs molds; changes cost more |
| Lead time | 35–50 days | 25–40 days |
| Best for | Wine brands, premium retail, decor | Supermarkets, hotels, promotions |

## When to choose hand-blown
- You sell on look and feel: crystal stemware, decanters, art vases
- You need colored, ombre or overlay effects
- You want to test a new collection without a large commitment

## When to choose machine-made
- You need 10,000+ identical pieces for chain stores or hospitality
- Stackability and exact capacity matter
- Price is the main purchase driver

## A mixed approach
Many buyers combine both: a machine-made core range for volume, plus hand-blown hero items for margin and brand image. We can source both from Shanxi and consolidate them into one shipment.

title: Borosilicate vs Soda-Lime vs Lead-Free Crystal: A Glass Material Guide for Importers
excerpt: Soda-lime is the low-cost everyday glass; borosilicate resists heat and thermal shock; lead-free crystal gives the best clarity and brilliance for stemware.
body:
**Short answer:** Use **soda-lime glass** for everyday tumblers and jars, **borosilicate glass** for hot drinks and cookware, and **lead-free crystal** for premium wine glasses and decanters.

## Comparison

| Property | Soda-lime | Borosilicate 3.3 | Lead-free crystal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main use | Tumblers, jars, vases | Teapots, mugs, storage, labware | Wine glasses, decanters, barware |
| Heat resistance | Low; avoid boiling water shocks | High (thermal shock ΔT ≈ 120 °C+) | Low–medium |
| Clarity and brilliance | Good | Good, slightly lighter feel | Excellent, higher refractive index |
| Weight | Medium | Light | Medium |
| Relative cost | $ | $$ | $$–$$$ |

## Soda-lime glass
Soda-lime is the most widely manufactured type of glass. It is inexpensive, recyclable and easy to color. It is not designed for sudden temperature changes.

## Borosilicate glass
Boron oxide lowers thermal expansion, so borosilicate tolerates hot liquids and temperature changes. It is the right choice for teapots, double-wall cups, coffee carafes and oven-safe containers.

## Lead-free crystal
Modern crystal replaces lead oxide with barium, zinc or titanium oxides. It gives high clarity, a fine ring and allows very thin rims. It is the preferred material for premium stemware.

## Compliance tips
- Ask for **food-contact test reports** (FDA for the US, LFGB for Germany, EU 1935/2004 for the EU)
- For decorated glass, test the **lip and rim area** for lead and cadmium release
- Specify the glass type in the purchase contract

title: How to Choose a Glass Perfume Bottle Supplier in China: A 10-Point Checklist
excerpt: Check five things before you pay a deposit: the neck finish fits your pump, the factory owns the mold, samples match production, decoration is done in-house or by a trusted partner, and packing is drop-tested.
body:
**Short answer:** A good perfume bottle supplier can show you the exact mold in stock, confirm the neck finish fits your pump, send production-grade samples, and explain who does each decoration step. If a supplier cannot answer these clearly, keep looking.

## The 10-point checklist

| # | What to check | Why it matters | What to ask for |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Mold ownership** | Stock molds are cheaper and faster; a new mold adds cost and 2–4 weeks | Photo or video of the bottle from the existing mold |
| 2 | **Neck finish** | A mismatch between bottle and pump is the most common perfume packaging failure | Neck drawing with size (e.g. 15 mm crimp / FEA 15) |
| 3 | **Glass weight and base thickness** | Heavy bases feel premium but affect cost and shipping weight | Weight in grams and a cross-section photo |
| 4 | **Capacity tolerance** | Brim-full and fill-level volumes differ | Brim capacity and recommended fill level |
| 5 | **Decoration route** | Spray coating, frosting, printing and hot stamping are often done by separate workshops | Who does each step, and where |
| 6 | **Color matching** | Spray colors shift between batches without a standard | Pantone reference and an approved color sample |
| 7 | **Closures as a set** | Bottle, pump, collar and cap from different vendors may not fit | A tested set: bottle + pump + collar + cap |
| 8 | **Quality standard** | Bubbles, stones, uneven bases and scratches are normal defects to control | AQL level and a defect list with photos |
| 9 | **Packing** | Heavy glass bottles break if cartons are weak | Inner dividers, carton strength, drop test |
| 10 | **Lead time** | Decoration and cap production often take longer than the glass itself | A schedule for each component |

## Red flags
- The "factory" cannot show the production line or the mold, only catalog photos
- Very low prices with no mention of the neck finish or glass weight
- No sample policy, or samples that differ from the quoted specification
- Decoration quoted without color approval

## How Shanxi fits in
Shanxi Province, especially the Qixian glass cluster, has decades of experience in glass forming, polishing and hand-finishing. Many perfume bottle factories in the region combine heavy-base flint glass with decoration such as [air-bubble effects](/products/perfume-bottles/air-bubble-glass-perfume-bottle-90-ml), [polished facets](/products/perfume-bottles/polished-faceted-glass-perfume-bottle-100-ml) and [spray-coated gradients](/products/perfume-bottles/spray-coated-gradient-perfume-bottle-100-ml).

title: Perfume Bottle Neck Finishes Explained: FEA 15 Crimp vs Screw Neck
excerpt: Crimp necks such as FEA 15 give the cleanest, most leak-resistant seal but need a crimping tool; screw necks are easier for small batches and refills. Always choose the pump and the bottle together.
body:
**Short answer:** Most fine-fragrance bottles use a **crimp neck**, most often **15 mm (FEA 15)**. The pump is crimped permanently onto the glass, which gives a clean look and a reliable seal. **Screw necks** (for example 18/415) let you close bottles by hand and allow refilling, which suits small batches, samples and refillable concepts.

## The main options

| Neck type | How the pump is fixed | Pros | Cons | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Crimp (e.g. FEA 13, 15, 18, 20)** | Metal ferrule of the pump is crimped around the glass neck | Slim, premium look; strong seal; collar hides the joint | Needs a crimping tool; not refillable | Eau de parfum, eau de toilette |
| **Screw neck (e.g. 18/415, 20/410)** | Pump screws onto a threaded neck | No machine needed; refillable; easy for small runs | Visible thread or bulkier collar | Samples, body mists, refillable lines |
| **Snap-on (no-crimp)** | Pump presses onto the neck | Fast filling without crimping | Fewer pump choices; check seal carefully | Mid-range and gift sets |

FEA is the code system used by the European perfume packaging industry for crimp neck sizes. The number refers to the neck diameter in millimetres.

## How to avoid fit problems
1. **Pick the pump and bottle together.** Ask the supplier to test the exact pump on the exact bottle.
2. **Check the dip tube length.** It must reach the bottom corner of the bottle. Heavy-base bottles have a raised inner bottom, so the tube is often shorter than you expect.
3. **Test the collar.** Decorative collars must sit flush on the shoulder and leave room for the cap.
4. **Approve a full set.** Approve bottle + pump + collar + cap together, then keep one set as the golden sample.

## Crimping in practice
Small brands can use a manual crimping tool for a few hundred bottles. For larger volumes, filling companies use pneumatic crimpers. Tell us how you plan to fill, and we will suggest the right neck.

Most bottles in our [perfume bottle range](/products/perfume-bottles) use a 15 mm crimp neck, for example the [clear heavy-base 100 ml bottle](/products/perfume-bottles/clear-heavy-base-glass-perfume-bottle-100-ml). Screw-neck versions are available on request. [Ask for a fitted sample set](/contact).

title: Custom Perfume Bottle Cost and MOQ: What Really Drives the Price
excerpt: The unit price of a perfume bottle is driven mainly by glass weight, whether a stock mold exists, decoration steps and the cap. Using a stock mold with your own color and logo is the fastest way to a low MOQ.
body:
**Short answer:** The biggest cost drivers are **(1) stock mold or new mold, (2) glass weight, (3) number of decoration steps, and (4) the cap**. If you start from a stock mold and customize the color, logo and cap, MOQs are usually in the low thousands and lead times stay around 30–45 days.

## Cost drivers, from biggest to smallest

| Driver | Effect on price | How to save |
|---|---|---|
| **New mold** | One-time mold fee plus 2–4 extra weeks | Start from a stock mold; customize it with decoration |
| **Glass weight** | Heavier bottles use more glass and cost more to ship | Choose the lightest base that still looks premium |
| **Decoration steps** | Each step (frosting, spray, printing, hot stamping) adds cost and some loss | Combine effects: e.g. a gradient spray plus one-color print |
| **Cap** | Zinc alloy and heavy acrylic caps can cost as much as the bottle | Surlyn or ABS caps with metallic finish |
| **Quantity** | Set-up costs are shared across the order | Group several sizes from one mold family |
| **Quality level** | Tighter defect limits mean more rejects | Agree on an AQL that matches your retail channel |

## Typical MOQ ranges
These are common starting points with Shanxi factories; the exact figure depends on the mold and decoration.

| Option | Typical MOQ |
|---|---|
| Stock mold, clear | about 3,000–5,000 pcs |
| Stock mold + spray color or print | about 3,000 pcs per color |
| Hot-fused or polished designs | about 2,000–3,000 pcs |
| Hand-made bottles | from about 500 pcs per design |
| New mold | usually 10,000 pcs or more to justify the mold |

## Lead time
- Stock bottles: about 20–30 days
- Decorated bottles: about 30–45 days
- New mold: add 2–4 weeks for mold making and samples

Caps and pumps are often the slowest part, so order them at the same time as the glass.

## How to get an accurate quote
Send capacity, target glass weight, neck finish, decoration, cap type, quantity per design, and destination. With that, we can quote stock-mold options from our [perfume bottle range](/products/perfume-bottles) within 1–3 working days. [Request a quote](/contact).

title: Glass Skincare Packaging Guide: Dropper Bottles, Pump Bottles and Cream Jars
excerpt: Use dropper bottles for oils and serums, pump bottles for lotions and emulsions, and wide jars for thick creams. Pick the glass color for your formula, and order the whole series from one supplier so finishes match.
body:
**Short answer:** Match the pack to the texture: **dropper bottles** for oils and thin serums, **pump bottles** for lotions and emulsions, and **jars** for thick creams and balms. For light-sensitive formulas, choose amber or fully coated glass. Order the whole series from one supplier so the color and finish match across sizes.

## Which pack for which product

| Product texture | Best pack | Typical sizes | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Facial oil, thin serum | Dropper bottle | 15–50 ml | Glass pipette doses precisely; check bulb material against your oils |
| Essence, toner | Bottle with orifice reducer or fine mist | 100–200 ml | Mist sprayers give a lighter application |
| Lotion, emulsion | Pump bottle | 30–120 ml | Treatment pumps for 0.2 ml doses; lotion pumps for larger doses |
| Cream, balm, mask | Wide-mouth jar | 15–100 g | Inner liner protects the formula and the cap |

## Glass finishes
- **Clear**: shows the product; best for stable, colorful formulas
- **Frosted**: soft, premium look; made by acid etching or spray
- **Solid or gradient color**: full brand color via spray coating, matched to Pantone
- **Pearlescent or electroplated**: metallic shine for prestige lines
- **Amber**: filters much of the light that can degrade sensitive ingredients

## Planning a full series
A launch usually needs a cleanser or toner, a serum, a lotion and a cream. Choosing one series from one supplier keeps the shoulder shape, glass color and cap finish consistent. See our [skincare glass packaging set](/products/skincare-cosmetic-bottles/skincare-glass-packaging-set-toner-lotion-cream).

## Compatibility tests to run
1. **Fill and leak test** with your actual formula, upside down for 24–48 hours
2. **Dose test** for pumps and droppers
3. **Decoration rub test** with your formula on the outside of the bottle
4. **Drop test** of the packed retail box
